```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| show_col_types: false

library(tidyverse)
library(skimr)
library(readxl)
library(janitor)
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)


WPE = read_csv("C:/Users/user/Documents/dsml/data/key-features-of-womens-political-empowerment.csv")

# Use to check code: 
WPE = clean_names(WPE)
# head(WPE[,1:7
#])

# Remove selected entities (don't exist after 1950) 

entity_to_remove <- c(
  "Duchy of Nassau",
  "Hanover",
  "Oldenburg",
  "Piedmont-Sardinia",
  "Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach",
  "Saxony",
  "Wurttemburg"
)


#limit the year from 1950 to 1990
WPE_country_clean <- WPE %>%
  filter(
    !entity %in% entity_to_remove,
    year >= 1950,
    year <= 2025
  )



#Rename Congo to Republic of Congo.
WPE_country_clean <- WPE_country_clean %>%
  mutate(
    entity = recode(
      entity,
      "Congo" = "Republic of Congo",
    )
  )

#Remove 'code' of countries
WPE_country_clean <- WPE_country_clean %>%
  select(entity,year, womens_political_empowerment_overall, womens_civil_liberties, womens_civil_society_participation, womens_political_participation)
```

## Taiwan v.s. Top 3 Asian Countries {.tabset}

### Political Empowerment Overall {width="75%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

WPE_top_asia <- WPE_country_clean %>%
  filter(
    entity %in% c(
      "Taiwan",
      "South Korea",
      "Japan",
      "Philippines"
    ),
    year >= 1950,
    year <= 2025
  )

WPE_top_asia <- WPE_top_asia %>%
  mutate(
    entity = factor(   #factor --> categorical variables 
      entity,
      levels = c(       #levels --> list of possible answers for categorical variables
        "Taiwan",
        "South Korea",
        "Japan",
        "Philippines"
      )
    )
  )

ggplot(
  WPE_top_asia,
  aes(x = year, y = womens_political_empowerment_overall, color = entity)                  #aes() --> aesthetic mappings
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(
    data = WPE_top_asia %>% filter(year == 2025),
    aes(label = entity),
    hjust = -0.1,          #horizontal justification
    size = 3,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Taiwan" = "firebrick",
      "South Korea" = "#00008B",
      "Japan" = "#00CD00", 
      "Philippines" = "#FF7F24"
    ),
    labels = c(
      "Taiwan",
      "South Korea",
      "Japan",
      "Philippines"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1950, 2025, by = 5),
    limits = c(1950, 2035)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Women's Political Empowerment: Taiwan v.s. Top 3 Asian Countries",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Overall Political Empowerment Score",
    color = "Country"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```

::: {.card width="25%"}
Women's political empowerment incorporates three equally-weighted dimensions:

- Fundamental civil liberties

- Women's open discussion of political issues and participation in civil society organizations

- The representation of women in formal political positions.

- In 2025, women's political empowerment overall:

  - Taiwan: 0.903

  - South Korea: 0.878

  - Japan: 0.844

  - Philippines: 0.810

This and the following graphs use data from Our World in Data, Women's Political Empowerment Index, which is produced by Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem). The index ranges from 0 to 1. It is made up of three sub-indices: [women's civil liberties](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/women-civil-liberties-index), [women's civil society participation](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/women-civil-society-participation-index), and [women's political participation](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/women-political-participation-index).
:::

::: {.card width="25%"}
Civil liberties measures if women have the ability to make meaningful decisions in key areas of their lives. It includes:

- Freedom of domestic movement

- The right to private property

- Freedom from forced labor

- Access to justice.

2025:

- Japan = 0.927

- South Korea= 0.926

- Taiwan = 0.925

- Philippines = 0.702
:::

Civil society participation asks if women have the **ability to express themselves** and to **form and participate in groups.** It includes:

- Open discussion of political issues

- Participation in civil society organizations

- Representation in the ranks of journalists

2025:

- South Korea = 0.812

- Japan = 0.715

### Analysis

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
library(tidyverse) 
library(skimr)
library(broom)
library(modelr)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: false

WPE_regression <- WPE_country_clean %>%
  select(
    entity,
    year,
    womens_civil_liberties,
    womens_civil_society_participation,
    womens_political_participation
  ) %>%
  drop_na()

model <- lm(
  womens_political_participation ~
    womens_civil_liberties +
    womens_civil_society_participation,
  data = WPE_regression
)

summary(model)
broom::tidy(model)


WPE_augmented <- broom::augment(    #augment adds columns to your original dataset
  model,
  data = WPE_regression
)

WPE_augmented %>%
  select(
    entity,
    year,
    .fitted,
    .resid
  ) %>%
  head()



# Residuals versus fitted values
plot(
  WPE_augmented$.fitted,
  WPE_augmented$.resid,
  xlab = "Fitted Values",
  ylab = "Residuals",
  main = "Residuals vs. Fitted Values"
)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2) #adds horizontal dash line at y = 0

# Normal Q-Q plot
qqnorm(WPE_augmented$.resid)
qqline(WPE_augmented$.resid)

```

::: {.card width="50%"}
**Coefficients**

|                             | Estimate  | Std. Error | t value | **Pr(\>\|t\|)** |
|---------------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
| Intercept                   | 0.203698  | 0.003672   | 55.48   | \< 2e-16        |
| Civil Liberties             | -0.234405 | 0.008757   | -26.77  | \< 2e-16        |
| Civil Society Participation | 1.029186  | 0.010016   | 102.75  | \< 2e-16        |

- Residual standard error: 0.1884 on 14168 degrees of freedom

- Multiple R-squared: 0.5576

- Adjusted R-squared: 0.5575

- F-statistic: 8929 on 2 and 14168 DF

- p-value: \< 2.2e-16

**Analysis**

The p-value \< 2.2e-16, so the probability of getting results at least as extreme is low. Therefore, we reject the null hypothesis. –\> It is **statistically significant**.

There is a **positive** correlation between [women's political participation]{.underline} and [civil society participation]{.underline}. Countries where women are more involved in civil society tend to also have more representation in formal political positions.

However, there is a **negative** correlation between [women's political participation]{.underline} and [civil liberties]{.underline} when civil society participation is taken into account. This result could be caused by differences between countries.

**Possible Explanations for Taiwan Being an Asian Outlier**

1.  The early adoption and gradual expansion of gender quota mechanisms. (CEIAS)
    - Explicit gender quotas in the 1946 Constitution of the Republic of China
    - Gradually broadened during the 1990s and early 2000s
    - Continuous reforms: Nov. 2025, amendment to Local Government Act (will take effect in 2030)
      - Raised the quota –\> 1 out of 4 to 1out of 3 seats must be for a woman
      - New gender-neutral formulation –\> 1 seat for a woman, 1 seat for a man, 1 seat unrestricted
2.  Key players taking advantage of the political climate
    - In 1987, martial law was lifted –\> allowed Taiwanese feminists to push for their own rights
    - **Annette Lu (呂秀蓮):** Taiwan's post-war pioneer feminist
      - Authored *New Feminism* in the 1970s
      - Called for revision of gender-biased family laws
      - Critiqued Confucian patriarchy
      - Elected to represent Taoyuan in the Legislative Yuan
      - Became Taiwan’s first female vice president in 2000
    - **Chen Chu (陳菊)**: the first woman to join the inner circle of Taiwan's Democracy Movement during the martial law era (1949 - 1987)
      - 1979 Kaohsiung Incident: one of two women among the eight staffers court-martialed
      - 1986: Co-founded the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP)

References:

1.  [Women's Political Empowerment Index, 2025](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/women-political-empowerment-index)

2.  [A quiet reform with big consequences: How Taiwan is reshaping women’s representation in local politics - CEIAS](https://ceias.eu/a-quiet-reform-with-big-consequences-how-taiwan-is-reshaping-womens-representation-in-local-politics/)

3.  <https://asiacentre.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/Asia-Sparks-Female-Power-in-Taiwanese-Politics.pdf>
:::
